summary: Specifies encoding of extensions to the IS-IS routing protocol for GMPLS. It is informational, and was replaced by RFC 5307.

eli5.summary: This memo describes extra fields in the IS-IS routing messages so they can describe optical network links. A newer RFC replaced it.

questions: how does gmpls advertise optical link capabilities
what is an interface switching capability descriptor
subtitle: Extending IS-IS to support optical label switching networks

tldr.problem: IS-IS is a routing protocol designed for IP networks, but GMPLS (Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching) controls both IP and optical/circuit-switched networks. Routers in GMPLS networks need to advertise information about the capabilities and availability of optical links, but IS-IS had no way to carry this information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4205 defines new TLVs (Type-Length-Value fields) and sub-TLVs for IS-IS that allow routers to advertise GMPLS-specific link information: link identifiers for unnumbered interfaces, protection mechanisms, interface switching capabilities (PSC, L2SC, TDM, LSC, FSC), bandwidth limits, and shared risk link groups for failure correlation.
tldr.outcome: This specification enabled IS-IS to serve as the routing protocol for unified IP/optical networks. It was superseded by RFC 5307, which added more switching types and enhanced the encoding.

today: RFC 4205 specified how IS-IS could advertise GMPLS network properties, enabling unified control of IP and optical networks. The specification was superseded by RFC 5307, which added more switching capability types (for spatial division multiplex and other technologies) and refined the encoding. Today, IS-IS with GMPLS extensions remains a foundation for service provider networks that integrate IP and optical switching.

sections.title: Why IS-IS Needs GMPLS Extensions
sections.content:
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is a routing protocol that exchanges network topology information between routers. Traditionally, IS-IS advertises IP-based link properties like bandwidth and cost. However, GMPLS (Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching) extends label switching beyond IP to control optical networks, circuit-switching networks, and time-division-multiplexed (TDM) networks.

In a GMPLS network, the routing and switching control planes must understand link capabilities that do not apply to pure IP networks: which wavelengths are available on optical links, whether a link can handle packet switching versus circuit switching, minimum and maximum bandwidth constraints, and which links share physical risk (so failures affect them together). RFC 4205 defines how IS-IS can carry this GMPLS-specific information by adding new TLVs and sub-TLVs to the IS-IS Link State Protocol Data Unit.
sections.eli5: IS-IS normally routes packets between routers. GMPLS also controls optical fiber networks. This RFC adds new labels to IS-IS messages so routers can tell each other about optical fiber properties—like 'this link can switch wavelengths' or 'this link can handle 100 Gigabits per second.'

sections.title: Core Extensions: Identifiers and Protection
sections.content:
RFC 4205 defines three main sub-TLVs within the IS-IS extended IS reachability TLV and one new top-level TLV. Link Local/Remote Identifiers (sub-TLV type 4) are 32-bit values that identify endpoints of unnumbered interfaces—interfaces that have no IP address and are identified only by their link-local ID. This is essential for GMPLS because optical links often do not have IP addresses.

Link Protection Type (sub-TLV type 20) is a 2-octet field that advertises the protection mechanisms available on a link: extra traffic, dedicated 1:1 protection, dedicated 1+1 protection, enhanced protection, or unprotected. This tells the GMPLS controller whether traffic on a link can be automatically rerouted on link failure or whether the link carries unprotectable traffic. The Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG) TLV (type 138) lists groups of links that share physical risk—for instance, multiple links using fibers in the same cable are all at risk if the cable is cut.
sections.eli5: These fields tell GMPLS routers: where this link starts and ends (IDs), how traffic is protected if the link fails (protection type), and which other links break if this one breaks (shared risk groups).

sections.title: Interface Switching Capability Descriptor
sections.content:
The Interface Switching Capability Descriptor (sub-TLV type 21) is the most complex extension. It specifies what types of traffic a link can switch and how much bandwidth is available. The descriptor begins with a Switching Capability field that identifies the link type: PSC-1 through PSC-4 (packet switch capable at different layers), L2SC (layer-2 switch capable), TDM (time-division multiplex for SONET/SDH), LSC (lambda switch capable for optical wavelengths), or FSC (fiber switch capable for whole fibers).

Following the switching capability, the descriptor lists Maximum LSP Bandwidth for each traffic priority (8 levels), encoded in IEEE floating-point format. A 4-octet field specifies bandwidth in bytes per second (not bits). For packet-switched and TDM links, additional fields specify the Minimum LSP Bandwidth and other parameters like interface MTU or SONET/SDH profile. A link can have multiple descriptors to indicate multiple switching capabilities (for example, a link that can switch both packets and wavelengths).
sections.eli5: This field tells GMPLS: 'I am a fiber link that can switch wavelengths (LSC). I can carry up to 10 Terabits per second for priority 0 traffic and 5 Terabits for priority 1.' Different link types need different information.

sections.title: Numbered and Unnumbered Interfaces
sections.content:
IS-IS traditionally uses IP addresses to identify link endpoints. In a GMPLS network, optical links often have no IP address. RFC 4205 supports both numbered interfaces (with an IPv4 address) and unnumbered interfaces (identified only by a local/remote identifier pair). The SRLG TLV includes a flag octet: the least significant bit is set to 1 for numbered interfaces and 0 for unnumbered interfaces.

For unnumbered interfaces, RFC 4205 specifies that link identifiers are exchanged in the Extended Local Circuit ID field of the IS-IS Point-to-Point Three-Way Adjacency option (RFC 3373), which establishes and confirms adjacencies between routers before they exchange routing information. This ensures that routers can reliably identify each other's interfaces even without IP addresses.
sections.eli5: Some links have IP addresses ('numbered'), like 198.51.100.5. Others have no IP address but have a link ID ('unnumbered'), like 'local ID 1234, remote ID 5678.' This field says which kind of link it is.

sections.title: Graceful Restart and Recovery
sections.content:
When a router running GMPLS restarts, it must not incorrectly advertise link capacity that is already reserved by established label switched paths (LSPs) that survived the restart. RFC 4205 specifies that a restarting node SHOULD advertise 0 unreserved bandwidth and, for optical links, 0 maximum LSP bandwidth, until it has rediscovered which LSPs were preserved during the restart.

This restart behavior prevents the GMPLS controller from allocating bandwidth on a link that is actually full. Similarly, when a restart is planned and scheduled in advance, the restarting router SHOULD pre-advertise 0 bandwidth to discourage new LSPs from being established through it before it restarts. Neighbors of the restarting node continue to advertise accurate resource information on links toward the restarting node, maintaining network visibility.
sections.eli5: When a router starts up again after crashing, it should announce 'I have no available bandwidth' until it knows which phone calls (LSPs) were already using my links. This prevents the network from sending new calls through an overloaded link.
